title: The First War of Independence, 1857
tagline: Causes, course, leaders and consequences of the first great uprising against Company rule.

overview.intro: The uprising of 1857 is the hinge on which the story of British India turns: it began as a sepoy mutiny in a cantonment and became a mass revolt across northern and central India, and when it was crushed the Company itself disappeared. This chapter separates the long-term causes from the immediate spark, traces the course of the revolt with the leaders of each centre, and then weighs the consequences — the transfer of power from Company to Crown and the end of a company on whose ships and armies an empire had been built. Cause-and-consequence is the examiner’s favourite work in this chapter, so the material is organised exactly in that shape.

facts.label: Date of the outbreak
facts.value: 10 May 1857, at Meerut, when the sepoys refused the new rifle cartridges and rose against their officers.

facts.label: The spark
facts.value: The Enfield rifle cartridge greased with cow and pig fat, which both Hindu and Muslim sepoys believed was designed to break their religion.

facts.label: Key centres
facts.value: Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah and Gwalior, each with its own leader.

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: The Government of India Act, 1858 ended Company rule; the Crown took over and Queen Victoria’s Proclamation promised non-intervention in religion.

learningOutcomes: Classify the political, economic, social, military and religious causes and separate them from the immediate cause.
Describe the outbreak at Meerut and the march to Delhi, and the role of Bahadur Shah II as the symbolic head.
Account for the conduct of the revolt in at least four centres with the names of their leaders.
Explain four consequences, including the transfer of power and the change in British policy towards the Princes.
Judge whether the revolt was a national uprising or a sepoy mutiny, giving reasons on both sides.

learn.title: The causes: political, economic, social, military and religious

blocks.text: The causes fall into five groups, and an answer that uses those five headings writes itself. Politically, the Doctrine of Lapse applied to Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Udaipur, Jaitpur, Sambalpur and Ambala, and annexations such as that of Awadh in 1856 on the charge of misgovernment alienated the Court of Awadh and its peasantry together, while the Subsidiary Alliance had already reduced many princes to dependants. Economically, the ruin of Indian handicrafts by machine-made imports threw artisans out of work, and the land revenue demand, often resettled at higher rates with moneylenders behind it, pressed hard on the peasant. Socially and religiously, missionary activity and the activities of reforming societies fed the belief that the Company intended to convert Indians, and legislation such as the abolition of sati and the Widow Remarriage Act, however beneficial in itself, was read by conservatives as interference with Indian religion. Administratively, the General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 required new recruits to serve overseas, which for a Hindu sepoy meant a loss of caste. Militarily, the sepoys were poorly paid, were denied the rewards given to British soldiers, and faced the new rifle cartridges whose grease became the immediate trigger.

items: Political: the Doctrine of Lapse, the annexation of Awadh in 1856 and the Subsidiary Alliance reducing princes to dependants.
Economic: destruction of Indian textiles and handicrafts by British manufactures, and a heavier, often increased, land revenue demand.
Social and religious: missionary activity and legislative interference feeding fears of forced conversion.
Administrative: the General Service Enlistment Act, 1856 requiring overseas service and threatening Hindu caste.
Military: low pay, limited promotions for sepoys, and the greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle.
Immediate cause: the new rifle introduced in 1856, whose cartridges had to be bitten open and were greased with cow and pig fat.

learn.title: The outbreak and the course of the revolt

blocks.text: On 29 March 1857 at Barrackpore, Mangal Pandey of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry attacked two British officers and was hanged, and the sepoys of that regiment were disbanded. On 10 May 1857 the sepoys at Meerut rose, shot their officers, released the imprisoned soldiers and marched to Delhi the next day, where they proclaimed the elderly Bahadur Shah II, the last of the Mughals, Emperor of India. The revolt then spread along the Ganges plain and into central India, with the main centres at Delhi under Bahadur Shah, Lucknow under Begum Hazrat Mahal, Kanpur under Nana Sahib and Tantia Tope, Jhansi and Gwalior under Rani Lakshmibai, Bareilly under Khan Bahadur Khan, and Arrah in Bihar under Kunwar Singh. The Company recovered by dividing its enemies: it offered amnesty to those who laid down arms, promised to respect the rights of loyal princes, and captured the key centres one by one. Delhi fell in September 1858 after a siege, Bahadur Shah was tried and exiled to Rangoon, Lucknow was relieved twice, Kanpur and Jhansi were taken, and Gwalior fell after the Rani died fighting in June 1858.

items: 29 March 1857: Mangal Pandey attacks his officers at Barrackpore; he is hanged and the 34th is disbanded.
10 May 1857: the Meerut sepoys rise, shoot their officers and march to Delhi.
11 May 1857: Bahadur Shah II is proclaimed Emperor of India at Delhi.
Main centres: Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah, Gwalior, Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand.
British recovery: amnesty to the obedient, protection of loyal princes, and the capture of each centre in turn.
Delhi, September 1858: the city falls after a siege and the King is tried and exiled to Rangoon.

learn.title: The leaders and the limits of their leadership

blocks.text: Each centre had a leader whose social position explains why people followed him or her. Bahadur Shah II was the last Mughal emperor, and for a population that still associated legitimacy with the throne his acceptance of a banner turned a local mutiny into a war of succession. Nana Sahib was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II, and claimed the pension Dalhousie had refused, so his grievance was personal and dynastic. Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi had been denied recognition for her adopted son under the Doctrine of Lapse and proved the most determined of the military leaders, dying in action at Gwalior. Kunwar Singh, an aged zamindar of Arrah, fought with the peasants and volunteers of Bihar and defeated a British force. Khan Bahadur Khan ruled for the minor Nawab of Rohilkhand, and Begum Hazrat Mahal took over the government of Awadh after the flight of her husband, Wajid Ali Shah. The limits are as instructive as the leadership: the rebels had no common programme, no shared ideology and no central command beyond Delhi, and many princes and zamindars stayed loyal, which is precisely why the British could isolate and defeat each centre in turn.

items: Bahadur Shah II: the last Mughal, accepted as Emperor of India, giving the revolt a unifying symbol.
Nana Sahib: the adopted son of Baji Rao II whose refused pension drove him to leadership at Kanpur.
Rani Lakshmibai: denied the succession for her adopted son under the Doctrine of Lapse; died fighting at Gwalior in June 1858.
Kunwar Singh: the zamindar of Arrah who led the Bihar rising and defeated British forces at nearly eighty years of age.
Begum Hazrat Mahal: took charge of Awadh after Wajid Ali Shah was deposed and ruled from Lucknow until its fall.
Tantia Tope: the guerrilla commander who kept the fighting alive in central India into 1859.

items.note: The Mughal throne was the oldest symbol of sovereignty in India, so the sepoys needed no persuading that a war fought under the Emperor’s banner was a lawful war rather than a rebellion.
Hyderabad, Patiala, Jodhpur, Gwalior and Indore remained with the British, and without their troops and treasuries the rebellion could not be sustained across the subcontinent.

blocks.text: The consequences run in three directions: the Company, the Crown and Indian society. The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred the governance of India from the East India Company to the British Crown, ended the Board of Control and the Court of Directors, and made the Secretary of State for India responsible to Parliament with an Indian Council of Advisors. Queen Victoria’s Proclamation of November 1857, read out at Allahabad in 1858, declared non-intervention in religion, promised respect for the rights and territories of Indian princes, promised employment irrespective of race and creed, and announced the end of the Doctrine of Lapse and of annexation. The army was reorganised so that the proportion of Indian soldiers to British soldiers was reduced, artillery and key garrisons were kept in British hands, and recruits were drawn from groups considered loyal. The policy towards the Princes hardened into a guarantee of their rights, which bought loyalty for the rest of British rule. Economic exploitation continued and in some respects deepened, so the revolt changed the form of rule without ending colonial exploitation.

items: Transfer of power: the Government of India Act, 1858 ended Company rule and made the Crown sovereign through a Secretary of State.
Queen’s Proclamation: non-intervention in religion, respect for princes, equal treatment for subjects and the end of the Doctrine of Lapse.
Army reorganisation: a smaller Indian proportion, no artillery for Indian troops and recruitment from supposedly loyal communities.
Policy towards the Princes: their rights and territories guaranteed, keeping the States out of later nationalist agitation.
Continued exploitation: land revenue and economic drain continued, so the ruler’s form changed but exploitation did not end.
A precedent: the scale of the uprising showed that British rule rested on consent as much as on force.

learn.title: Was it a national uprising or a sepoy mutiny?

blocks.text: This is the judgement question that closes the chapter, and it is best answered by putting the two cases in turn and then naming the deciding evidence. That it was more than a mutiny: the revolt embraced a wide territory from Punjab to Bengal and from Delhi to central India, drew in peasants, artisans, zamindars and displaced rulers as well as sepoys, had leaders of different regions and communities, was given a symbol in the aged Mughal emperor, and was followed by the transfer of an entire government. That it fell short of a national movement: there was no common programme, no ideology of unity and no centrally directed plan; large parts of the south and the west never rose; loyal princes supplied the troops that crushed it; and most leaders were displaced rulers seeking the return of their own privileges rather than the liberty of India. The balanced judgement examiners accept is therefore that it was a widespread popular revolt with a strong sepoy core, which awakened both the rulers and the ruled to the realities of colonial power, but it was not yet a national movement in the organised sense that the Congress became after 1885.

items: For a national uprising: wide territory, participation of all classes, a symbol in the Mughal throne, and a transfer of government as the result.
Against: no common programme, no unity of leadership, southern and western India outside it, and leaders seeking restoration of their privileges.
The balanced judgement: a widespread popular revolt with a sepoy core that shook Company rule but was not an organised national movement.
Its lasting importance: it ended Company rule and forced a policy of non-intervention and guarantee towards the princes.

items.note: Define the two terms first, then give three arguments for each side with instances, and close with a one-line balanced verdict rather than an unsupported preference.

questions.explanation: The Meerut sepoys rose on 10 May 1857; Barrackpore was the earlier Mangal Pandey incident of 29 March.

questions.prompt: The immediate cause of the revolt was:
options: The greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle
questions.answer: The greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle
questions.explanation: The greased cartridges were the trigger; the other three are underlying causes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following leaders belonged to Kanpur?
questions.explanation: Nana Sahib, with Tantia Tope, led the rising at Kanpur; Kunwar Singh led Arrah and Khan Bahadur Khan led Bareilly.

questions.prompt: The act that transferred the governance of India from the Company to the Crown was:
questions.explanation: The Government of India Act, 1858 carried the transfer into law; the Proclamation stated the policy.

questions.prompt: The last Mughal emperor, proclaimed Emperor of India by the revolting sepoys, was Bahadur Shah __________.
questions.explanation: Bahadur Shah II was tried and exiled to Rangoon after the fall of Delhi in September 1858.

questions.prompt: The Doctrine of __________ denied an Indian ruler without a natural heir the right to adopt a successor without British permission.
questions.explanation: The doctrine was applied to Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and other states and drove rulers such as Rani Lakshmibai into revolt.

questions.prompt: State any three economic causes of the revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: First, Indian handicrafts and textiles were ruined by machine-made British goods, which threw artisans and weavers out of work. Second, the land revenue demand was often increased at resettlement and exacted through moneylenders, pressing the peasant hard. Third, wealth extracted through trade and revenue enriched Britain while Indian producers lost their livelihood, so the economic grievance cut across the countryside and the towns alike.
questions.explanation: The three economic strands are the ruin of industry, the heavier revenue demand and the drain of wealth.

questions.prompt: How did the British succeed in crushing the revolt?
questions.answer: They followed a policy of divide and rule: amnesty was offered to all who laid down their arms, the rights of the princes to their states were publicly guaranteed, and Indians who remained loyal were taken into confidence, which split the rebels from the moderate chiefs. Militarily they concentrated on the key centres one after another — Delhi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Jhansi and Gwalior — using their superior artillery and their control of the roads and river routes, so each centre fell separately rather than in a single battle.
questions.explanation: Amnesty and guarantees divided the rebels, while the sequential capture of each centre destroyed them one by one.

questions.prompt: Mention two promises made in Queen Victoria’s Proclamation of 1857.
questions.answer: The Proclamation promised non-intervention in the religious beliefs and practices of Indians, and it promised respect for the rights, dignity and territories of the Indian princes. It also declared an end to the Doctrine of Lapse and to annexation, and promised employment in the service of the Crown without racial or religious discrimination.
questions.explanation: Religious non-intervention and the guarantee to the princes are the two most frequently marked promises.

questions.prompt: Explain the political and military causes of the revolt of 1857 and show how the immediate cause gave them a common expression.
questions.answer: Politically, the Doctrine of Lapse deprived rulers without natural heirs of the right to adopt, and was applied to Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Udaipur, Jaitpur, Sambalpur and Ambala, so several ruling families lost their thrones. The annexation of Awadh in 1856 on the charge of misgovernment displaced the Nawab and a whole body of officials, tenants and retainers, and the Subsidiary Alliance had already turned independent rulers into dependants. Militarily, the sepoys of the Bengal Army were poorly paid, were denied the promotions and rewards given to European soldiers, and were forbidden the badges they had been allowed for distinguished service; the General Service Enlistment Act of 1856 required overseas service, which for Hindu sepoys meant the loss of caste. The immediate cause gave all of this a single expression: the new Enfield rifle of 1856 required cartridges to be bitten open, and the rumour that they were greased with cow and pig fat convinced both Hindu and Muslim sepoys that the British intended to break their religion, so a religious fear united grievances that were otherwise political, economic and military.
questions.explanation: Each political and military cause must be named with an instance, and the cartridge rumour shown as the unifying trigger rather than as a cause on its own.

questions.prompt: Was the revolt of 1857 a national uprising? Give arguments for and against and state your judgement.
questions.answer: Arguments for a national uprising: the revolt spread across a vast territory from Punjab to Bengal and from Delhi to central India; it drew sepoys together with peasants, artisans, zamindars and displaced rulers; leaders of different regions and communities fought under a single symbol in the aged Mughal emperor; and its consequence was the transfer of an entire government, which no mere mutiny could achieve. Arguments against: there was no common programme, no ideology and no central direction beyond Delhi; the south and much of the west did not rise; many princes and zamindars remained loyal and supplied the troops that suppressed the uprising; and most leaders were displaced rulers seeking the restoration of their own privileges rather than the freedom of the people. My judgement is therefore that the revolt was a widespread popular uprising with a sepoy core, which showed that British rule depended on consent as much as force and ended Company rule, but it was not yet a national movement in the organised sense in which the Indian National Congress became one after 1885.
questions.explanation: Both sides must be argued with instances and closed with a balanced verdict that names what the revolt achieved and what it lacked.

questions.prompt: Why did the British maintain a policy of respect and friendship towards the Indian princes after 1858?
questions.answer: The princes had largely stayed loyal during the revolt, and their troops, treasuries and prestige had been essential in suppressing it, so the British concluded that the princes were a stabilising interest rather than a threat. The Proclamation of 1857 promised respect for their rights and territories, and the Government of India Act, 1858 gave that promise the force of policy by ending the Doctrine of Lapse and the practice of annexation. Friendship with the princes also secured a counterweight to the growing educated and nationalist classes: a ruler who owed his throne to British protection could be relied upon to support the government in the councils and in times of unrest. The policy therefore turned potential opponents into allies and gave the Crown a constituency of loyalty across India for the rest of British rule.
questions.explanation: Loyalty during the revolt, the guarantee of the Proclamation and the strategic counterweight against nationalist opinion together explain the policy.
